terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. Run the night report here and read the error Python prints.

tasks.title: Bring back the callouts
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 1` in `night_report.py`, the line that prints the callouts this month stops Python before anything prints. Run the file, read the error, and fix that line so it prints `Callouts this month:` followed by the number in `callouts_this_month`, as the comment above it shows.

Check runs your file with other numbers in `callouts_this_month` and looks for that line among the lines Task 1 prints. The line that makes `callouts_this_month` stays as it is.
nextSteps: Run `python3 night_report.py` and read the first line of the error: it ends with a line number.
Look at the copy of that line and the `^` under it.
Read the kind of error on the last line, then compare the line with the example in the comment above it.
Fix the line and run the file again. A new error is good news: it is the next task.
hints: The number after `line` in the first line of the error is the line to look at. The `^` shows where Python got lost.
A `SyntaxError` about a string that never ends means a text starts with a quote and the quote that should close it is missing. Where should this text end?
The text is only `Callouts this month:`. The line has the shape `print("...", callouts_this_month)`.

tasks.title: Bring back the hours on the hill
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 2`, the line that prints the hours on the hill stops Python too. Fix it so it prints `Hours on the hill:` followed by the number in `hours_on_the_hill`.

Check runs your file with other numbers in `hours_on_the_hill` and looks for that line among the lines Task 2 prints.
nextSteps: Fix Task 1 first: Python reads the whole file before it runs any of it, so it stops there first.
Run the file and read the kind of error on the last line.
Look at the very start of the line it names, and compare it with the lines around it.
Fix it and run the file again.
hints: The error does not complain about any word on the line. It complains about where the line starts.
`unexpected indent` means a line starts further right than Python expects. A line that is not inside anything starts at the very left edge.
Remove the spaces in front of `print` on that line, so it starts in the same place as the line above it.

tasks.title: Bring back the kit officer
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 3`, the line that prints the kit officer stops Python while the file runs, after the lines above it have printed. Fix it so it prints `Kit officer on call:` followed by the name in `kit_officer`.

Check runs your file with other names in `kit_officer` and looks for that line among the lines Task 3 prints.
nextSteps: Run the file once Tasks 1 and 2 are fixed, and see which lines print before the error.
Read the traceback from the bottom: the kind of error and the name it does not know.
Compare that name, letter by letter, with the line that makes the variable.
Fix it and run the file again.
hints: This error comes from a line that Python could read but not run. Read the last line of the traceback first.
A `NameError` names a variable Python does not know. Look for the line that makes that variable: are the two spelt the same?
The line should use `kit_officer`, spelt exactly as on the line above it.

tasks.title: Bring back the crew on call
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 4`, the line that prints the crew on call stops Python too. Fix it so it prints `Crew on call:` followed by the number in `crew_on_call`, with one space between them.

Check runs your file with other numbers in `crew_on_call` and looks for that line among the lines Task 4 prints, spaces included.
nextSteps: Run the file and read the last line of the traceback.
Ask what kind of value sits on each side of the `+`.
Pick one of the ways the lessons showed to print text and a number together.
Fix it, run the file and check the space after the colon.
hints: A `TypeError` means a value of the wrong kind was used. The message says which two kinds met.
`+` can join text to text, but `crew_on_call` is a number. `print` can also take the text and the number as two values, with a comma between them.
Either `print("Crew on call:", crew_on_call)`, or join with `+` after turning the number into text with `str`.
